title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Kernel Scheduling, Profiling Playbook, Benchmarks, Runbooks, and Team Wiki
author: Arielle Chen
content:
Overview

This consolidated reference describes the Redwood Serving Runtime architecture, kernel scheduling model, profiling and benchmarking practices, operational runbooks, and the team wiki guidance for on-call and performance investigations. The document is intended as the single-source-of-truth for engineers and SREs operating and evolving the inference runtime.

Goals
- Communicate the architecture and key tradeoffs driving scheduling and kernel selection.
- Provide step-by-step profiling/playbook guidance for latency and throughput investigations.
- Document the benchmarking suite and standard workloads used for performance regressions.
- Consolidate runbooks and escalation paths for production incidents.

Scope
Covers hosted and dedicated inference runtimes (GPU-based), including the kernel selection layer, batching and KV cache subsystems, and the observability instrumentation used for SLOs. This doc does not cover private on-prem packaging details (see eng-private-deployments).

1) Runtime architecture (summary)

High-level components:
- Frontend API gateway: ingress, auth, basic quota checks. Responsible for routing to appropriate fleet (hosted/dedicated/private).
- Router / Smart Routing: policy layer for cost/latency/region-based routing and fallback to model variants.
- Request broker: converts API requests into scheduling units and applies per-customer queueing rules.
- Scheduler & kernel selector (local to each node): chooses batching strategy and kernel configurations based on model metadata, sequence length, temperature, and hardware characteristics.
- Execution engine (serving runtime): runs optimized kernels, manages KV cache, handles streaming, and returns tokens.
- Telemetry / Observability: per-request traces, token-level cost/latency breakdowns, and per-route dashboards.

Key design points:
- Separation of routing and scheduling allows lightweight routing policy changes without touching per-node scheduling heuristics.
- Deterministic fallback policies minimize variance during capacity constraints.
- Strong telemetry at token granularity is required to accurately attribute cost and detect regressions.

Architecture table (short):
| Component | Owner | SLOs | Notes |
|-----------|-------|------|-------|
| Frontend API | eng-platform | 99.95% p99 request acceptance | Handles auth and initial validation |
| Router | eng-serving-runtime | 99.9% decision latency < 10ms | Supports policy exchange |
| Scheduler / Selector | eng-serving-runtime | 99% batch selection < 30ms | Local heuristics + model profiles |
| Execution engine | eng-serving-runtime | p99 per-token latency targets depend on model profile | GPU-optimized kernels, batching |

2) Kernel scheduling and batching model

Overview
The scheduler runs on each GPU node and performs three responsibilities: (1) select the batching window, (2) pick a kernel/quantization configuration, and (3) schedule KV-cache placement for multi-GPU contexts. Scheduling decisions use metrics and profiles in the model catalog and recent per-node latency/occupancy stats.

Principles:
- Latency SLOs are prioritized for p99-sensitive routes (real-time chat). Throughput-focused routes (bulk generation) prefer larger batches and lower cost kernels.
- Workload-aware batching: prefer heterogeneous batches only when latency impact is bounded; otherwise prefer homogeneous batching for deterministic kernels.
- Kernel selection uses a three-tier lookup: exact model profile -> similar-arch fallbacks -> default stable kernel set.

Scheduling heuristics (summary):
1. Classify incoming requests by route priority (realtime|interactive|batch).
2. Check KV cache hit probability; cache hits can bypass full execution and use fast-path kernels.
3. Compute target batch size using current GPU occupancy, recent p50/p95 latencies, and per-route latency budget.
4. If target batch < threshold, pick low-latency kernel (FP16 fused ops). Else pick throughput-optimized kernel (quantized kernel with batched matmuls).
5. Record selection and metrics to telemetry for feedback.

Example pseudo-policy:
- If route.priority == realtime and p99_latency_recent > SLO -> target_batch = max(1, current_batch - 1) and kernel = low-latency.
- If occupancy < 40% and queue_depth > 0 -> increase batch up to occupancy-driven cap.

3) Profiling playbook (for performance regressions)

When a performance regression is detected (alert from dashboards / regressions test), follow this playbook:

Triage steps (ordered):
1. Confirm the signal
   - Check per-route p50/p95/p99 graphs and token-level latency breakdowns.
   - Verify alert scope: single node, AZ, region, or global.
2. Reproduce on staging
   - Use the benchmarking harness (see section 4) with the same model version and request shape.
   - Run synthetic workload matching median sequence length and temperature.
3. Narrow to subsystem
   - Inspect node-level metrics: GPU utilization, memory, kernel runtime distribution (top kernels by time).
   - Check KV cache hit rate and prefix cache evictions.
4. Kernel-level analysis
   - Capture per-kernel timings via the profiler (nvprof/NSight-like integration) and compare against baseline.
   - Look for increased memcopy time, unexpected syncs, or kernel fallback choices.
5. Revert / mitigate
   - If a model change introduced the regression, roll back to the previous model variant for impacted routes using the rollout system.
   - If scheduler heuristics are the cause, roll forward incremental scheduler config with canary on 1 AZ.
6. Postmortem
   - Document root cause, timeline, impact, and required follow-ups. Update model profiles or kernel configs as needed.

Profiling commands (examples)
- Run the local stage harness: ./tools/benchmark --model my-model --seq-len 512 --concurrency 8 --profile=perf.json
- Collect trace from node: /usr/local/bin/collect-trace --duration 60s --out /tmp/trace.json

Required telemetry to collect:
- per-request token latency breakdown (queueing, kernel, memcopy, serialize)
- per-kernel percentiles and invocation counts
- GPU occupancy and SM utilization by kernel family

4) Benchmarking suite and standard workloads

Purpose
Benchmarks are used for admission testing (new kernel/driver/quantization), release validation, and regression detection. The suite is runnable in CI and on isolated staging clusters.

Standard workloads included:
- chat_realtime_light: seq_len=64, temp=0.8, token_budget=128, concurrency=16 (realtime SLO test)
- chat_interactive: seq_len=256, temp=0.7, token_budget=256, concurrency=8 (default interactive)
- batch_generation: seq_len=1024, temp=1.0, token_budget=512, concurrency=4 (throughput focused)
- embeddings_mini: embedding_size=1536, batch_size=64 (embeddings throughput)

Artifacts produced by a run:
- latency_summary.json (p50/p95/p99 per-request and per-token)
- kernel_profile.csv (kernel timing distribution)
- occupancy_report.csv (GPU occupancy over time)

CI gating rules
- No PR may merge if the p99 for any realtime workload increases > 7% vs baseline.
- Throughput regressions > 10% for batch workloads must be investigated and justified.

5) Release notes (runtime changes and recommendations)

Guidelines for runtime releases:
- Each runtime release must include a summary of kernel changes, driver updates, and model profile changes.
- Attach benchmark artifacts and CI comparisons.
- Note any required action for downstream teams (e.g., model owners should re-run evals if quantization baseline changed).

Example release summary (template):
- Version: 2027.12.08
- Highlights: Added fused attention kernel for long context models (improves p95 by 18% on seq=2048).
- Known impacts: small increase in memcopy for FP16 fallback path.
- CI results: realtime p99 -1.2%, batch throughput +4.6%.

6) Known issues (current)

Active items (as of last_updated):
- ISSUE-2027-417: Under certain driver 535.* builds, the matmul quantized kernel may return non-deterministic timings causing scheduler to oscillate. Mitigation: pin driver to 534.88 until vendor patch. Owner: runtime-kernel-team.
- ISSUE-2027-488: KV cache eviction policy sometimes evicts useful prefixes under high-concurrency multi-tenant workloads resulting in p95 regressions. Mitigation: temporary per-tenant cache quotas. Owner: cache-team.
- ISSUE-2027-510: Embedding batcher misreports batch sizes in telemetry under heavy load; leads to incorrect billing attribution. Owner: observability-team.

If you hit one of the above in production, follow the runbook in section 7 and tag the incident with the issue ID.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)

A) High p99 latency on realtime routes
1. Verify alert scope (route/region/node).
2. Check recent deployments: model, runtime, scheduler config. If rollout within last 60 minutes, consider automatic rollback.
3. SSH to a representative node and run: curl http://localhost:9100/metrics | grep serving_runtime
4. Validate GPU metrics: gpu_util, sm_efficiency, mem_used.
5. If kernel times are high, add a temporary route-level override: max_batch=1 and kernel_hint=low_latency via the runtime config API.
6. Open an incident and page runtime-ctrl/eng-sre.

B) Node OOMs during compilation
1. Identify node and model being compiled (compile logs: /var/log/compile-agent.log).
2. If OOM happened during just-in-time kernel compilation, increase compile timeout and retry on a larger instance type.
3. If persistent, blacklist model on that instance family and route to alternate family.

C) Degraded KV cache hit rate
1. Inspect prefix cache metrics for eviction rate and top prefixes evicted.
2. Apply temporary per-tenant cache quota increases for critical tenants.
3. Recompute and push updated cache admission thresholds via the config service.

8) Team wiki and onboarding notes

Where to find resources:
- Kernel development guide: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/kernel-and-scheduling
- Benchmarking harness repo: git.internal/redwood/serving-benchmarks (README includes run instructions)
- Profiling tools and dashboards: Dashboards -> Serving Runtime -> Profiling (link)

On-call tips:
- First 10 minutes: stabilize (reduce batch sizes, pin kernels, roll back recent model changes).
- First 30 minutes: determine root cause class (scheduler vs kernel vs infra).
- Always attach latency breakdown traces to the incident; token-level breakdown speeds diagnosis.

9) Ownership and escalation

Primary owners:
- runtime-kernel-team (kernel selection and kernel changes)
- runtime-scheduler-team (batching heuristics and config)
- cache-team (KV cache policies)
- eng-sre (on-call escalation, infra capacity)

Escalation path:
1. Pager: runtime-urgent -> runtime-lead -> eng-sre -> infra-oncall -> exec on-call (for severity=1).

Appendix: quick CLI and config examples

- Update scheduler override (example):
  curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
    https://config-api.internal/runtime/scheduler/overrides \
    -d '{"route":"/v1/chat","max_batch":1,"kernel_hint":"low_latency"}'

- Run benchmark locally:
  ./tools/benchmark --config workloads/chat_realtime_light.yaml --iterations 100 --out runs/run-$(date +%s)

- Interpreting kernel_profile.csv: columns: timestamp, kernel_name, duration_ms, gpu_id, invocation_count

Document maintenance
- Please update this page for any change that affects runtime scheduling, kernel releases, or benchmark definitions.
- Major edits require at least two reviewers from the reviewers list.

End of document.
